answer.rationale: Finance demands an 18% cost cut and the primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew. The assembly line has no buffer, so delivery risk must not increase. Memory_c1 and memory_c6 together indicate that staying with the incumbent preserved integration stability and that multi-year commitments unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope. Memory_c4 shows that negotiating at renewal recovered real margin through benchmarking against market rates, improving both price and payment terms. A switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2) might cut unit cost further but introduces onboarding and delivery risk at a moment when the line has zero buffer, violating the delivery-risk constraint. Adding a second source (memory_c3) addresses resilience but does not directly address the 18% cost mandate and would likely increase spend. Deferring (memory_c5) is not viable because the contract does not auto-renew; deferral creates a coverage gap. Therefore, negotiate_terms with the incumbent, using multi-year commitment as leverage for volume pricing and market-rate benchmarking to push both price and payment terms, is the single action that targets cost reduction while preserving the stable, interruption-free delivery the incumbent has demonstrated. Verifying memory_c6 confirms the multi-year pricing mechanism before committing.
